draft.body:
# Who gets to tell the story?

## Reading the scene

I first read Mara leaving the porch as an escape. On my second reading, the cup she leaves behind complicated that answer. A person can leave a house and still keep its habits. The narrator notices the cup but never tells us what Mara thinks. That gap is where my reading starts. I do not want to turn a small detail into a secret code with only one solution. Instead, the cup lets me ask whether departure is something the family recognizes only afterward.

## A competing reading

Mara explicitly says that she will never return. This proves she has rejected every relationship in the village. Yet the final image is an unlatched gate, which might leave return possible. I need to decide whether these details conflict or whether my claim asks the story to be tidier than it is. The gate matters to me because the sentence slows down there. It makes the leaving feel unfinished, like a conversation someone has walked out of before either person can answer.

## What remains open

My claim is that the ending holds departure and attachment together. I would not describe Mara as either liberated or trapped without qualification. Those words name possibilities, but the story makes us sit between them. I still hear the cup touching the table after the paragraph ends. That is the effect I want my argument to explain.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.body: The brief requires a contestable claim, but the claim is not made until this final section ("the ending holds departure and attachment together"). The opening section, "Reading the scene," only sets up the gap and poses a question, so the reader does not learn what is being argued until the last 57 words. For a 400-word close reading, the claim belongs in the opening; as ordered, the argument is buried at the end, and this section is the shortest of the three, underdeveloped relative to the setup.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: # Who gets to tell the story?
comments.body: The top-level heading frames the piece as an argument about narrative authority — who gets to tell the story — but the sections actually argue about departure versus attachment (the cup, the gate, the ending holding two things together). The only reference to narration is the narrator's gap in "Reading the scene," which is never developed into a claim. The heading promises an argument the body does not make, so it does not serve the brief's required claim. (Judgment: how the heading reads against the argument the sections actually land on.)

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: Mara explicitly says that she will never return.
comments.body: This claim is not supported by any recorded excerpt from the story, and it is likely invented dialogue. The only recorded excerpt from source 1 ("The Unlatched Gate") has Mara "crossed the yard without speaking," and no excerpt records her saying she will never return. The brief explicitly forbids inventing dialogue. This line is the load-bearing claim of the "competing reading" section — the whole contrast (definite departure vs. the unlatched gate) rests on it — so if the line is invented, the section collapses. It is also presented as a flat fact about the text rather than a quotation, which blurs the line the brief asks you to keep between quoted narration and interpretation. Verify the line against the full text and quote it if it exists; remove it if it does not.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: This proves she has rejected every relationship in the village.
comments.body: "This proves she has rejected every relationship in the village" overclaims on two counts. A single line does not "prove" anything so broad, and "every relationship in the village" generalizes beyond the text into the biographical context the brief says not to invent. Even granting the preceding statement, the inference is stronger than the evidence supports. Scale this down to what the line actually establishes (e.g., that Mara has declared an end to her ties), and drop "proves."

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: I need to decide whether these details conflict or whether my claim asks the story to be tidier than it is.
comments.body: This sentence refers to "my claim" before the claim is stated — the claim ("the ending holds departure and attachment together") is not made until section 1.3. A claim should be stated before it is referenced, or this reference should be removed. As ordered, the reader is asked to weigh "my claim" against the details without knowing what it is, which undercuts the move. State the claim earlier (or reword so it does not depend on a claim the reader has not yet been given).

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: On my second reading, the cup she leaves behind complicated that answer.
comments.body: The cup does not appear in the only recorded passage from "The Unlatched Gate" ("She pulled the porch door shut and crossed the yard without speaking."), and the source ledger has no excerpt supporting it. This section's central detail is therefore unverifiable from the recorded source, and the brief forbids adding context the text does not give. The student needs to confirm the cup is actually in the excerpt and record the exact passage it relies on, or remove the detail.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: Instead, the cup lets me ask whether departure is something the family recognizes only afterward.
comments.body: "The family" is biographical context the recorded source does not establish — the only recorded passage mentions just "She." The brief explicitly forbids inventing biographical context. The student needs to ground the family in a recorded passage from the excerpt or remove the reference.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: I first read Mara leaving the porch as an escape.
comments.body: The name "Mara" does not appear in the recorded source excerpt, which refers to the character only as "She." The student should record the passage that names her so the name is verifiable against the source.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The narrator notices the cup but never tells us what Mara thinks.
comments.body: "Never tells us what Mara thinks" is a claim about the whole excerpt, but the only recorded passage is a single sentence ("She pulled the porch door shut and crossed the yard without speaking."), which addresses speech, not interiority. The word "never" is stronger than the recorded evidence supports, and the section's "gap" argument depends on it. The student should verify the claim against the full excerpt or soften the language.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The narrator notices the cup but never tells us what Mara thinks.
comments.body: The brief asks the reader to distinguish quoted narration from interpretation, but this section never quotes the excerpt — it paraphrases ("the cup she leaves behind," "the narrator notices the cup"). Quoting the actual sentence(s) the claims rest on would let the reader separate what the text says from what the student is reading into it.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The gate matters to me because the sentence slows down there.
comments.body: "Matters to me" is vague, and "the sentence slows down there" asserts a rhythmic effect the reader cannot verify from what is given. Either show what in the sentence produces the slowing, or state the effect more modestly.
